prompt: A procurement proposal claims more devices alone will create an integrated C2 capability. Which challenge is strongest?
options: C2 becomes complete when every item has a serial number
Organizational and information integration also matter
Human responsibilities disappear after hardware installation
Device quantity always measures decision quality directly
explanation: The system-of-systems concept requires functioning organizational and information relationships, not inventory alone.

prompt: Reliable transport and fast processing are demonstrated, but users receive unusable information. What has not been established?
options: The measured processing speed in the demonstration
The existence of the tested transport link
The presence of the demonstrated computers
The integrated information purpose
explanation: Component performance is insufficient if the resulting information does not support the intended users.

prompt: A report merges observations and conclusions without distinguishing them. What should the assessment require?
options: Clear separation of collected evidence and analytical judgment
Removing all source observations from the record
Treating every observation as a conclusive interpretation
Assigning certainty according to the report's page count
explanation: Collection and analysis are related but distinct; readers need to understand the evidential basis of conclusions.

prompt: A network outage is described as proof that command authority ceased to exist. What correction is appropriate?
options: A router failure transfers command to the equipment vendor
Authority exists only while every device is online
The computer with the newest software inherits authority
Technical failure does not erase authority
explanation: Technical systems support command, but command is an assigned authority and responsibility.

prompt: A shared picture looks consistent because conflicting reports were silently discarded. What is the concern?
options: Discarding all disagreement guarantees completeness
Consistency of appearance proves the picture is accurate
Visual agreement may conceal unresolved evidence quality
The number of displayed symbols establishes truth
explanation: A coherent display is not enough if its apparent certainty hides unresolved or excluded evidence.

prompt: An automated exchange bypasses established permissions to reduce delay. Which review is necessary?
options: Remove accountability because the process is automated
Assume lower latency authorizes every information transfer
Preserve authorized access and responsibility alongside timeliness
Treat connectivity as consent from all information owners
explanation: Timeliness does not override authorization or institutional responsibility.

prompt: A report satisfies a basic observation need but is reused for a purpose demanding greater accuracy. What must be checked?
options: Whether a faster network can make its original content more exact
Whether its information quality meets the new requirement
Whether its original file name remains unchanged
Whether copying it into a new template creates sufficient detail
explanation: Information suitability depends on the intended use; transfer or reformatting does not improve underlying accuracy.

prompt: Feedback arrives after the displayed situation has changed, but its age is ignored. What assumption is unsafe?
options: That users should understand the limits of available evidence
That received feedback necessarily describes the current situation
That information age can matter to interpretation
That updated observations may change an assessment
explanation: Delivery does not establish currency; decision-makers need to understand information limitations.

prompt: Every internal system is replaced with one brand, yet staff procedures remain incompatible. What follows?
options: Interoperability has no connection to staff practices
One vendor automatically standardizes every human process
Organizational differences cannot affect information exchange
Uniform equipment does not prove complete interoperability
explanation: The lesson includes people and processes; technical uniformity alone cannot satisfy the whole concept.

prompt: Two services use the same interface label but incompatible implementation options. What should acceptance examine?
options: Whether a common label makes every implementation equivalent
Only whether the label is capitalized identically
Only whether both suppliers describe their products as modern
The agreed profile and actual implementation behavior
explanation: Interoperability profiles specify options and standards; labels alone do not establish conformance.

prompt: Packet delivery succeeds, but values are interpreted differently by the receiving system. Which test is missing?
options: Only the availability of power to the network device
Correct end-to-end interpretation of exchanged information
Only the sender's ability to connect a cable
Whether packet delivery can replace all interface documentation
explanation: Transport success must be complemented by semantic and application-level correctness.

prompt: An interface change is made without coordinating dependent systems. What is the principal integration risk?
options: Existing consumers may no longer interpret the exchange correctly
Interface documentation becomes unnecessary after the first release
Open architecture guarantees all changes are backward compatible
A newer format automatically updates every remote consumer
explanation: Defined interfaces create dependencies; changes need coordination and compatibility validation.

prompt: A supplier equates open architecture with anonymous access. Which response is correct?
options: Only proprietary systems need access restrictions
Open architecture prohibits every form of authentication
Published standards automatically authorize every user
Extensible interfaces still require appropriate security controls
explanation: Openness concerns architectural interoperability and extension, not unrestricted information access.

prompt: A design uses TCP/IP and encryption but omits recipient authorization. What can be concluded?
options: Access governance remains incomplete
Encryption replaces the need to identify intended recipients
Every security requirement is satisfied by those two features
TCP/IP determines who has a legitimate need-to-know
explanation: Networking and encryption are not substitutes for authorization and access control.

prompt: All individual components pass tests, but a shared network dependency fails the integrated service. What did component tests miss?
options: The existence of individual user manuals
The fact that each component had a test result
System-level availability dependencies
The physical presence of the tested devices
explanation: Integration introduces relationships and dependencies that individual component tests may not exercise.

prompt: A planned upgrade improves exchange but removes segmentation. What should the review balance?
options: Functional interoperability with security requirements
Only whether the new interface uses fewer words
Only the highest possible count of connected devices
The assumption that more connectivity always means more security
explanation: Interoperability and protection must be designed together; functional improvement does not excuse lost safeguards.

prompt: An architecture is evaluated without its intended environment or users. What is the main limitation?
options: Actors and information structure are merely decorative labels
A framework is valid only if it contains no people
Suitability cannot be judged from technical elements alone
Every operational context imposes identical requirements
explanation: The source explicitly relates architecture to environment, actors, processes and information structure.

prompt: Historical delivery milestones are presented as proof of present-day readiness. What qualification is necessary?
options: Historical diagrams are substitutes for all present validation
Once acquired, equipment can never develop support dependencies
Past acquisition is not current readiness
A recorded delivery date guarantees indefinite operational readiness
explanation: Milestones document development history, not a current readiness assessment.

prompt: A classroom configuration diagram is offered as a complete implementation instruction. Why is that inadequate?
options: Labels alone guarantee correct implementation by any user
A conceptual diagram omits required specifications, authority and validation
Every diagram necessarily contains every operational parameter
A diagram removes the need for approved technical documentation
explanation: Conceptual relationships support learning but do not replace authorized specifications and validated implementation.

prompt: Which assessment best fits the lesson's integrated-system objective?
options: Check useful information exchange, roles, interfaces and protection together
Verify one connection and assume every service behaves identically
Rank systems only by the amount of data they can display
Count installed devices and ignore how people use the information
explanation: The lesson integrates components and organizational roles through usable, secure information exchange.
